question: In the same file, a neighbour who witnessed the will is married to the family friend who receives the $8,000 gift under the will. Two other unrelated people also witnessed the signing at the same time. Is the $8,000 gift to the family friend affected by the rule against gifts to witnesses, given this marriage?

options.A: It is void, because the neighbour personally received a benefit himself.
options.B: It is not void, because two witnesses remain unconnected to that gift.
options.C: It is not void, because only a gift made directly to a witness counts.
options.D: It is void, because a gift to a witness's spouse is typically forfeited.

explanation: The correct answer is B (It is not void, because two witnesses remain unconnected to that gift.): The forfeiture rule catches a gift to a witness or to that witness's then spouse, so the gift to the family friend is caught because the neighbour who witnessed the will is married to her. The same exception applies again here, because the cousin and the colleague are both unconnected to the family friend's gift and were also attesting witnesses. Since two independent witnesses remain, the gift to the family friend is not void.

question: The cousin from this file, whose own gift was discussed above, is later asked to give evidence proving the testator properly executed the will. Does the fact that the cousin received a gift under the will stop her from acting as a witness for this purpose?

options.B: No, but a judge must also be present at trial for her evidence.

explanation: The correct answer is D (No, a witness who receives a gift remains competent to prove the will.): The statute is explicit that a beneficiary witness remains a competent witness to prove the will, even though the underlying gift to that person may be affected. Competence to give evidence about execution and entitlement to keep a gift are treated as two separate questions. No rule requires a judge to be present for the cousin's evidence to be admissible.

question: The lawyer in this file used three witnesses out of caution, even though the will could have been executed with fewer. As a matter of Ontario law, how many witnesses are actually required for a typewritten will to be validly executed?

options.B: Two witnesses who are both present when the testator signs or acknowledges.
options.C: Four witnesses if the estate includes real property located in Ontario.
options.D: One witness, provided the signature is later notarized by a commissioner.

explanation: The correct answer is B (Two witnesses who are both present when the testator signs or acknowledges.): A typewritten will requires only two attesting witnesses who are present at the same time when the testator signs or acknowledges the signature, and who then sign the will themselves in the testator's presence. Using a third witness, as this lawyer did, is a common practice for extra safety but is not legally required. Notarization and the number or size of assets in the estate have no bearing on the number of witnesses needed.

question: A testator signs his name in the margin beside the last paragraph of his will rather than directly underneath the final words, because he ran out of room on the page. The rest of the will is otherwise properly witnessed. A family member later argues the will fails because the signature is not at the very bottom of the page.

options.A: The will fails, because a margin signature is an unwitnessed alteration.
options.B: The will stands only once retyped with more space at the bottom.
options.C: The will stands, because a signature beside the end can still give it effect.
options.D: The will fails, because a signature generally must sit under the final line.

explanation: The correct answer is C (The will stands, because a signature beside the end can still give it effect.): Ontario law does not require the signature to sit at the exact physical bottom of the page, and a signature placed at, after, beside or opposite to the end of the will is sufficient as long as it is clear the testator meant to give effect to the document as a will. A margin signature placed this way is not treated as an unwitnessed alteration, since nothing about the wording itself was changed after signing. Retyping the document is unnecessary on these facts.

question: A man dies in 2026 leaving an unsigned, never witnessed note on his computer that clearly sets out how he wanted his cottage and his savings divided between his two children. His family applies to the Superior Court of Justice, arguing the note plainly shows his intentions. What can the court do about it?

options.A: It must automatically accept the note once it is filed for probate.
options.B: It may accept the note only once notarized by a commissioner of oaths.
options.C: It may order the note effective if satisfied it shows his true intentions.
options.D: It has no power to validate a document that was not signed.

explanation: The correct answer is C (It may order the note effective if satisfied it shows his true intentions.): Since 2022, the Superior Court of Justice has a substantial compliance power that lets it declare a document effective as a will where it is satisfied the document sets out the deceased's genuine testamentary intentions, even though it was never properly executed. This power is discretionary rather than automatic, so the family still needs to satisfy the court on the evidence rather than simply filing the note. No notarization step is part of this substantial compliance process.

question: A testator tells her lawyer over the phone that she wants to cancel her existing will, but she never signs any new document, never destroys the original, and never puts anything in writing about cancelling it. She dies the following month. Has her earlier will been revoked?

options.A: No, a will is only revoked by a later will, writing, or destruction.
options.B: Yes, a clear statement of a changed intention cancels the earlier will.
options.C: Yes, a clear verbal instruction to a lawyer revokes an existing will.
options.D: No, but only because the lawyer failed to write down the call.

explanation: The correct answer is A (No, a will is only revoked by a later will, writing, or destruction.): Ontario law lists a closed set of ways to revoke a will, being a later qualifying will, a written document declaring revocation and made with the same formalities as a will, or destruction of the will with the intention to revoke it. A spoken instruction to a lawyer, without any of those steps actually being carried out, does not revoke anything. Whether the lawyer took notes of the call is irrelevant, since none of the recognized methods of revocation were used.

question: A testator's will leaves $100,000 to his spouse and the rest of his estate to a charity, but his life insurance names no beneficiary, so $500,000 passes as an intestate asset. He is survived by his spouse and one child, and the preferential share is $350,000. How is that insurance money treated?

options.A: The spouse takes the shortfall needed to reach the preferential share first.
options.B: The spouse receives nothing further since she already has a gift.
options.C: The charity receives the amount too, in addition to its residue gift.
options.D: The child receives the entire amount since it was not mentioned in the will.

explanation: The correct answer is A (The spouse takes the shortfall needed to reach the preferential share first.): Where a person dies partly testate and partly intestate and the spouse receives less than the preferential share under the will, the spouse is entitled to take the shortfall out of the property that passes on intestacy. Here the spouse's $100,000 gift is $250,000 short of the $350,000 preferential share, so she takes that shortfall from the insurance proceeds before anyone else shares in them. The child and the charity only share in whatever remains once the spouse's preferential share has been topped up.

question: A testator left his whole estate to a charity, but for years before his death he had been paying his disabled adult daughter's rent and also supporting his unemployed brother with monthly payments. Which of these two relatives is capable of qualifying as a dependant entitled to claim support against this estate?

options.A: Both of them qualify as dependants he was supporting before his death.
options.B: Only the daughter qualifies, since a brother is rarely treated as a dependant.
options.C: Only the brother qualifies, since an able bodied adult child is excluded.
options.D: Neither qualifies, since the will names a charity instead of family.

explanation: The correct answer is A (Both of them qualify as dependants he was supporting before his death.): A dependant includes a child of the deceased and a brother or sister of the deceased, but only where the deceased was providing support, or was under a legal obligation to provide support, immediately before death. Both relatives here were receiving regular financial support from the testator right up until his death, so both can qualify. The fact that the will leaves everything to a charity does not remove either relative's status as a dependant, it is exactly the situation the support claim exists to address.
cluster_text: A testator died on March 1 leaving a will that gave his entire estate to a local charity. For the three years before his death, he had been paying his adult daughter's rent and medical costs because a permanent disability prevents her from working. He had also been giving his unemployed brother $500 a month for the eighteen months before his death to help cover living costs. Letters probate were granted on May 1. By the following January, seven months after the grant, most of the estate had been distributed to the charity, but a $40,000 parcel of land had not yet been transferred.

question: Letters probate on this estate were granted on May 1. Assuming no extension is granted and no part of the estate remains undistributed, by what date would an application for dependant support ordinarily have to be made, counting from that grant?

options.A: By November 1, six months after the letters probate were granted.
options.B: By September 1, four months after the letters probate were granted.
options.C: By March 1 of the next year, one full year after the death.
options.D: There is no deadline once a claim rests on monthly support payments.

explanation: The correct answer is A (By November 1, six months after the letters probate were granted.): The statute sets the ordinary limitation period for a dependant support application at six months after the grant of letters probate, which here means six months after May 1, landing on November 1. The date of death itself is not the trigger for this deadline, only the date the grant is issued. A deadline does apply here regardless of how the underlying support was structured, whether as monthly payments or otherwise.

question: It is now seven months after the grant of letters probate on this estate, so the six month deadline has already passed, but a $40,000 parcel of land has not yet been transferred to the charity. Can the daughter or the brother still bring a claim against this estate at this point?

options.A: A claim is only possible now if the charity consents in writing.
options.B: A claim is only possible if the estate trustee applies for an extension.
options.C: No claim is possible now, since the six month deadline has expired.
options.D: The court may still allow a claim against the undistributed land if fair.

explanation: The correct answer is D (The court may still allow a claim against the undistributed land if fair.): Even after the ordinary six month deadline has passed, the court may allow a late application if it considers it proper, but only as to any part of the estate that is still undistributed at the date of the application. Since the $40,000 land has not yet been transferred, that undistributed portion remains available for a late claim. Neither the charity's consent nor an application by the estate trustee is a precondition to the court exercising this discretion.

question: Besides the daughter and the brother themselves, the family wants to know who else is permitted under the statute to bring a dependant support application on behalf of a person like either of them, given how the support was actually provided in this case.

options.A: Only another named beneficiary may bring the application for a dependant.
options.B: Only the estate trustee may bring the application for a dependant.
options.C: Only a lawyer retained directly by the dependant may bring it.
options.D: The dependant's parent, or certain public agencies providing support.

explanation: The correct answer is D (The dependant's parent, or certain public agencies providing support.): The statute allows the application to be made by the dependant or by the dependant's parent, and it also permits certain listed public agencies to apply if they are providing, or have provided, income support or similar benefits to that dependant. A retained lawyer acts on the dependant's instructions rather than being a separate applicant in his or her own right. Neither the estate trustee nor another beneficiary has any special standing under this provision to bring the claim.

question: An estate trustee is compiling the value of the estate for the statement required on a probate application. The deceased held a joint bank account with his adult son that passes by survivorship, and also owned a TFSA with a named beneficiary designation. Should these two assets be included in the estate value?

options.A: No, survivorship assets and a TFSA with a beneficiary designation are excluded.
options.B: Only the TFSA must be included, the joint account is generally excluded.
options.C: Only the account must be included, a TFSA is typically excluded automatically.
options.D: Yes, every asset the deceased held any interest in must be included.

explanation: The correct answer is A (No, survivorship assets and a TFSA with a beneficiary designation are excluded.): Assets that pass to a surviving joint owner by right of survivorship, and registered accounts such as a TFSA with a valid beneficiary designation, are both excluded from the value of the estate for this tax. Neither category needs a court order or election to be excluded, the exclusion follows automatically from how the asset is legally held or designated. Combining these two facts, both assets described here fall outside the value that the estate trustee must report.

question: An estate trustee is deciding whether an estate can use the simplified small estate certificate procedure instead of the full probate process. The deceased's assets, once properly valued, total $148,000. Is this estate eligible for the small estate procedure under the current regulation?

options.A: No, the small estate procedure only applies to estates under $50,000.
options.B: Yes, but only if every beneficiary named in the will is an adult.
options.C: No, a small estate certificate is generally not available when real property is involved.
options.D: Yes, the estate does not exceed the $150,000 prescribed small estate limit.

explanation: The correct answer is D (Yes, the estate does not exceed the $150,000 prescribed small estate limit.): A small estate is defined as one that does not exceed the amount prescribed by regulation, which is currently $150,000, so an estate valued at $148,000 qualifies for the simplified procedure. The $50,000 figure belongs to a different rule, the estate administration tax exemption threshold, and should not be confused with the small estate ceiling. Nothing in the small estate rules requires every beneficiary to be an adult, though special notice steps apply where a beneficiary is a minor.

question: An estate trustee wants to file for a small estate certificate for an estate worth $120,000. One of the beneficiaries named in the will is fourteen years old. The trustee has not yet sent the application or the will to anyone and wants to file with the court tomorrow morning.

options.A: The trustee cannot file while any beneficiary is a minor.
options.B: The trustee can file tomorrow, since notice only applies to adult beneficiaries.
options.C: The trustee can file tomorrow, since the Children's Lawyer only gets notice later.
options.D: The trustee must first give 30 days notice to the parent and Children's Lawyer.

explanation: The correct answer is D (The trustee must first give 30 days notice to the parent and Children's Lawyer.): An application for a small estate certificate cannot be filed until at least 30 days after the applicant has sent the application and the will to every person entitled to share in the distribution, and where a beneficiary is under 18 the documents must also go to a parent or guardian and to the Children's Lawyer. Filing tomorrow, before that notice has even been sent, would be premature regardless of the estate's size. A minor beneficiary does not block the small estate process entirely, it simply triggers this additional notice requirement before filing.

question: A grantor wants his adult son to witness the continuing power of attorney for property that names the son's spouse as the attorney. The grantor's lawyer needs to advise whether the son is permitted to witness this document given who the named attorney is.

options.A: He can witness it, as long as the grantor confirms consent in writing.
options.B: He cannot witness it, since any relative of the grantor is barred.
options.C: He cannot witness it, since a spouse of the named attorney is barred.
options.D: He can witness it, since only the attorney personally is barred.

explanation: The correct answer is C (He cannot witness it, since a spouse of the named attorney is barred.): The statute bars several categories of people from witnessing a continuing power of attorney for property, including the attorney and the attorney's spouse or partner, so the son cannot witness a document naming his own spouse as attorney. Written consent from the grantor does not override this statutory bar. The bar is not a blanket rule against any relative of the grantor witnessing, since a child of the grantor is only barred in that separate capacity, not because relatives in general are excluded.

question: A grantor in a rural hospital wants to sign a continuing power of attorney for property before surgery, using a video call with two witnesses joining remotely. A month later, before the surgery happens, she executes a brand new continuing power of attorney naming a different attorney entirely. What is the effect of the second document on the earlier one?

options.A: It has no effect, because a grantor may generally hold only one power of attorney at a time.
options.B: It is invalid, because a power of attorney typically cannot replace an earlier one.
options.C: It suspends the first power of attorney until the grantor later confirms which one applies.
options.D: It terminates the first power of attorney, since a new one revokes the earlier grant.

explanation: The correct answer is D (It terminates the first power of attorney, since a new one revokes the earlier grant.): A continuing power of attorney terminates when the grantor executes a new continuing power of attorney, unless the grantor has provided for multiple continuing powers of attorney to operate together. Nothing here suggests the grantor intended to keep both documents alive at once, so the later one simply supersedes the first. The remote execution of the first document was valid in its own right, since audio visual signing is permitted where a witness is a licensee, but that validity does not stop a later document from ending it.

question: A lawyer is meeting with a client who wants to give a continuing power of attorney for property to her son. Under the statutory test of capacity to give such a document, what must the client understand about the attorney's role and her own ongoing obligations?

options.A: That the document generally cannot be revoked once it has been properly signed and witnessed.
options.B: That the power of attorney can only be exercised after a court order is obtained.
options.C: That the attorney will automatically become her guardian once she signs the document.
options.D: That the attorney must account for dealings and that she may revoke it while capable.

explanation: The correct answer is D (That the attorney must account for dealings and that she may revoke it while capable.): A person is capable of giving a continuing power of attorney if she knows, among other things, that the attorney must account for dealings with her property and that she may revoke the power of attorney while she remains capable of doing so. Signing the document does not turn the attorney into a court appointed guardian, and no court order is needed before the attorney can act. The capacity test exists precisely because the power takes effect without ongoing court supervision unless something later goes wrong.

question: A lawyer is assessing whether a client is incapable of personal care under the statutory test. Which two things must the client be shown to be unable to do, relating to decisions about health care, nutrition, shelter, clothing, hygiene or safety, before a finding of incapacity is proper?

options.A: Recall the names of every doctor or care provider she has ever consulted.
options.B: Communicate clearly, or express a firm preference between two competing options presented to her.
options.C: Live independently, or manage most basic daily tasks without significant outside assistance.
options.D: Understand relevant information, or appreciate the foreseeable consequences of a decision.

explanation: The correct answer is D (Understand relevant information, or appreciate the foreseeable consequences of a decision.): A person is incapable of personal care where the person cannot understand information relevant to a decision about health care, nutrition, shelter, clothing, hygiene or safety, or cannot appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of making or not making that decision. This is the same understanding and appreciation framework used for property decisions, just applied to personal care topics instead. Being unable to live independently, recall every provider's name, or communicate a firm preference are not themselves the statutory test.

question: A lawyer is confirming that a client has capacity to give a power of attorney for personal care before the meeting ends. Under the statutory test, what must the client be able to understand and appreciate before the document can validly be signed by her?

options.A: That the attorney will generally make sound medical decisions on her behalf.
options.B: That a court must approve the document before the attorney may begin to act.
options.C: That the attorney is legally required to be a licensed health care professional.
options.D: That the attorney genuinely cares for her and may need to make decisions.

explanation: The correct answer is D (That the attorney genuinely cares for her and may need to make decisions.): A person is capable of giving a power of attorney for personal care if she can understand whether the proposed attorney has a genuine concern for her welfare and can appreciate that she may need the attorney to make decisions for her. Nothing in the test requires the attorney to make flawless decisions, be a licensed professional, or obtain prior court approval before acting. The focus is on the grantor's own understanding of the relationship, not on guaranteeing a particular outcome.

question: An attorney has been managing property under a continuing power of attorney for two years, because the grantor became incapable of managing property shortly after signing it. What ongoing obligation does the attorney have regarding records of the property transactions during this period?

options.A: The attorney must keep accounts of all transactions involving the property.
options.B: The attorney must file annual accounts directly with the Superior Court of Justice.
options.C: The attorney has no accounting obligation as long as no complaint is ever raised.
options.D: The attorney only needs to keep records once the grantor's death actually occurs.

explanation: The correct answer is A (The attorney must keep accounts of all transactions involving the property.): Once the grantor is incapable of managing property, or the attorney has reasonable grounds to believe so, the attorney is under a duty to keep accounts of all transactions involving the grantor's property, whether or not any complaint has yet been raised. The accounts do not need to be filed automatically with the court every year, they are instead produced if a passing of accounts is later required. The duty to keep records begins during the grantor's incapacity, not only once the grantor has died.

question: A surviving spouse is deciding whether to take under her late husband's will or to claim the equalization entitlement under the Family Law Act instead. She takes no formal steps and simply lets time pass without filing anything with the Estate Registrar for Ontario. What happens if six months pass with no election filed?

options.A: She is deemed to have elected to take under the will absent a court order.
options.B: She generally loses her entitlement to inherit from the estate.
options.C: The estate trustee may choose whichever option seems most convenient for the estate.
options.D: The equalization entitlement is granted to her automatically by default instead.

explanation: The correct answer is A (She is deemed to have elected to take under the will absent a court order.): The election must be filed with the Estate Registrar for Ontario within six months after the spouse's death, and if no election is filed in that time, the surviving spouse is deemed to have elected to take under the will, unless the court orders otherwise on application. This deeming rule does not strip her of everything, it simply locks in the will based option by default. The estate trustee has no power to pick between the two options on the surviving spouse's behalf.

question: A taxpayer dies owning shares in a public company that have grown significantly in value since he bought them, with no special rollover provision applying to this particular property. Under the general rule for capital property at death, what is the taxpayer deemed to have done with the shares immediately before death?

options.A: Disposed of them for proceeds equal to what he originally paid for them.
options.B: Disposed of them for proceeds equal to their fair market value immediately before death.
options.C: Retained them indefinitely until the shares are eventually sold by the estate.
options.D: Transferred them tax free to whoever inherits them under his will.

explanation: The correct answer is B (Disposed of them for proceeds equal to their fair market value immediately before death.): Where a taxpayer dies, he is deemed to have disposed immediately before death of each capital property, including shares like these, and to have received proceeds equal to the fair market value of that property immediately before death. This deemed disposition is what typically triggers a capital gain, since it compares fair market value rather than the original purchase price. Absent a specific rollover, the property is not transferred tax free, and it is not simply treated as retained until an eventual future sale.

question: A deceased owned shares of an ordinary small business corporation that does not carry on any farming or fishing activity. His will leaves those shares to his adult daughter. Does a general rollover on death let those shares pass to the daughter without triggering the deemed disposition rule?

options.A: No, because shares are rarely permitted to be transferred to a child.
options.B: Yes, every transfer of private company shares to a child rolls over automatically.
options.C: No general rollover exists for ordinary small business shares passing to a child.
options.D: Yes, because any shares held for more than five years qualify for a child rollover.

explanation: The correct answer is C (No general rollover exists for ordinary small business shares passing to a child.): The rollovers to a child in the federal tax legislation are specifically for farm and fishing property, and for shares of a family farm or fishing corporation, not for ordinary small business corporation shares with no farming or fishing activity. Since these shares do not meet the farm or fishing definitions, they remain subject to the ordinary deemed disposition rule on death, though the lifetime capital gains exemption may still reduce the resulting tax. The shares can certainly still be transferred to the daughter, the transfer itself is not what is being denied.

question: A deceased annuitant under an RRSP dies after the plan matured, and the entire fair market value of the plan becomes receivable by his surviving spouse. What tax treatment is potentially available for that amount when it is paid to the spouse?

options.A: It may be treated as a refund of premiums, reducing the deemed amount in his income.
options.B: It is largely tax free to the estate no matter who ultimately receives it.
options.C: It is generally taxable in full to the deceased no matter who receives it.
options.D: It must be reported only on the spouse's own final tax return instead.

explanation: The correct answer is A (It may be treated as a refund of premiums, reducing the deemed amount in his income.): Where the value that becomes receivable by the spouse reduces the amount the deceased annuitant is deemed to have received immediately before death, that reduction is described as a refund of premiums, and the legal representative and the spouse may jointly designate the payment for this treatment. The amount is not simply always fully taxable with no relief, nor is it automatically tax free, the refund of premiums mechanism is what determines the actual result. Reporting obligations here run through the deceased's own return and the joint designation, not solely through the spouse's separate return.

question: A deceased held a TFSA that named her adult son as the successor holder. She also had a separate non registered investment account with no joint owner or beneficiary designation at all. How are these two assets treated for estate administration tax purposes?

options.A: The TFSA is excluded from the value, while the investment account is included.
options.B: The TFSA is included, while the investment account is excluded from the value.
options.C: Both assets are excluded from the estate value because both are investments.
options.D: Both assets are generally included in the estate value despite any designation.

explanation: The correct answer is A (The TFSA is excluded from the value, while the investment account is included.): A TFSA with a valid beneficiary or successor holder designation passes outside the estate and is not included in the value of the estate for this tax, while an ordinary investment account with no such designation and no joint owner falls into the estate and must be included at its date of death value. Both assets being investments does not by itself exclude either of them, the designation is what matters. The two assets are treated differently here precisely because only one of them carries a valid designation.

question: An estate arising on a person's death qualifies as a testamentary trust and designates itself as the graduated rate estate in its first tax return filed after 2015. For how long after the death can this estate continue to be treated as a graduated rate estate under the definition?

options.A: Until a clearance certificate is finally issued by the Canada Revenue Agency.
options.B: No more than 36 months after the death, provided no other requirement is missed.
options.C: For about 12 months after the death, independent of when administration finishes.
options.D: Indefinitely, as long as the estate remains open and continues to be administered.

explanation: The correct answer is B (No more than 36 months after the death, provided no other requirement is missed.): A graduated rate estate exists only where, among other conditions, the relevant time is no more than 36 months after the individual's death, along with the estate being a testamentary trust and meeting the social insurance number and self designation requirements. The status is not indefinite, it is not fixed at 12 months, and it does not depend on when a clearance certificate happens to be issued. Once 36 months have passed, the estate can no longer be treated as a graduated rate estate under this definition.

question: An estate trustee wants to distribute the remaining assets of the estate to the beneficiaries, but the final personal income tax return has just been filed and no clearance certificate has yet been received from the Canada Revenue Agency. What risk does the trustee face if she distributes now?

options.A: Only the beneficiaries who receive property become liable, not the trustee herself.
options.B: She faces criminal liability automatically the moment any distribution is made early.
options.C: She can become personally liable for unpaid tax up to the value of the property distributed.
options.D: She faces little risk as long as the tax return itself was accurate.

explanation: The correct answer is C (She can become personally liable for unpaid tax up to the value of the property distributed.): A legal representative who distributes estate property without first obtaining a clearance certificate can be held personally liable for unpaid amounts owed under the Income Tax Act, up to the value of the property distributed. An accurate return does not remove this risk, since the certificate confirms all outstanding amounts have actually been paid or secured, not merely reported correctly. This is a personal liability risk for the representative herself, not simply a criminal offence, and it falls on the trustee rather than only on the beneficiaries.

question: A settlor tells her lawyer she wants to set up a trust for her grandchildren but has not yet decided exactly which property will fund it or precisely who among her many relatives will benefit. For a valid express trust to later exist, what must eventually be certain about the trust besides the settlor's intention to create one?

options.A: The trust property must be identified, and the beneficiaries or purpose must be identified.
options.B: The trust must last for at least twenty one years once it is created.
options.C: The trustee must be a licensed professional trust company rather than an individual.
options.D: The trust must be registered with a government office before it can exist.

explanation: The correct answer is A (The trust property must be identified, and the beneficiaries or purpose must be identified.): A valid express trust requires the three certainties, being certainty of intention, certainty of subject matter meaning the trust property is identified, and certainty of objects meaning the beneficiaries or charitable purpose are identified. Nothing in this common law requirement demands government registration or a licensed corporate trustee, an individual trustee is perfectly capable of holding a valid trust. A minimum twenty one year duration is not part of the three certainties either, that concept belongs to the separate rule against perpetuities.

question: A solicitor is asked how the estate administration tax is calculated for an application for an estate certificate. The application is made in 2026 and the value of the estate is well above $50,000. Which description of the rate matches the Estate Administration Tax Act, 1998?

options.A: $0 on the first $50,000, then $15 for each $1,000 above it.
options.B: $5 on the first $50,000, then $15 for each $1,000 above it.
options.C: $5 for each $1,000 of the whole value, with no exemption.
options.D: A flat $15 for each $1,000 of the whole value of the estate.

explanation: The correct answer is A ($0 on the first $50,000, then $15 for each $1,000 above it.): For an application made on or after January 1, 2020, the first $50,000 of value is exempt and the tax is $15 for each $1,000, or part thereof, by which the value exceeds $50,000. The older split rate of $5 and $15 applied to applications made before January 1, 2020 and does not apply to this application. A flat charge on the whole value would tax the first $50,000, which the current rule exempts.

question: The estate trustee is preparing the application for a certificate of appointment of estate trustee with a will and must deposit the estate administration tax. Using the values given in the scenario, what amount of estate administration tax is payable on those facts?

options.A: $6,450, being $15 for each $1,000 above $50,000.
options.B: $6,270, which deducts the unpaid funeral bill from the value of the estate.
options.C: $7,800, which adds the value of the jointly held shares to the estate.
options.D: $9,150, which does not deduct the mortgage from the value of the house.

explanation: The correct answer is A ($6,450, being $15 for each $1,000 above $50,000.): The value of the estate is the house at its date of death value less the mortgage that charges it, plus the bank account, which gives $480,000. Property held in joint tenancy with a surviving joint tenant passes by survivorship and is not included in the value of the estate. Funeral expenses are not deductible in arriving at the value, so the tax is $15 for each $1,000 above $50,000, or $6,450.
cluster_text: Doreen died in February. Her will named her daughter Maya as estate trustee and divided the residue equally between Maya and her brother Peter. At the date of death Doreen owned a house worth $620,000 that was subject to a mortgage of $180,000, and a bank account of $40,000 in her own name. She also held shares worth $90,000 in joint tenancy with her son Paul, who survived her. Doreen's funeral bill of $12,000 was unpaid at the date of death, and her final income tax return had not been filed. In May, before paying the funeral bill and before obtaining a clearance certificate, Maya paid the whole residue to herself and Peter. Maya has not yet filed the estate information return and gave no notice to creditors.

question: Maya distributed the whole residue before obtaining a certificate from the Minister confirming that all amounts for which she may become liable have been paid or secured. If the estate is later assessed for income tax under the Income Tax Act, what is her position?

options.A: She is protected because no creditor gave notice before the distribution.
options.B: The beneficiaries become liable instead, because they received the property.
options.C: She is personally liable for the unpaid tax to the extent of the value distributed.
options.D: She is liable only for the estate administration tax, which the estate owes.

explanation: The correct answer is C (She is personally liable for the unpaid tax to the extent of the value distributed.): A legal representative who distributes property without first obtaining the Minister's clearance certificate is personally liable for the amounts unpaid, to the extent of the value of the property distributed. That liability is personal to the representative and does not shift to the beneficiaries merely because they received the property. Notice from creditors does not displace the Income Tax Act rule, and estate administration tax is owed by the estate rather than by the representative personally.

question: Before distributing, Maya published notices asking creditors and others to send in their claims by a stated time, as the Superior Court of Justice would have directed in an administration suit. What protection does that give her under the Trustee Act?

options.A: She is not liable for assets distributed where she had no notice of the claim.
options.B: She is protected only if the estate was insolvent when she distributed.
options.C: The protection covers assets she still holds but not assets already paid out.
options.D: She is protected from all creditors, and their claims are extinguished.

explanation: The correct answer is A (She is not liable for assets distributed where she had no notice of the claim.): A personal representative who gives the notices that the Superior Court of Justice would have directed in an administration suit may distribute, having regard to the claims then known, and is not liable for assets distributed to a person of whose claim there was no notice at the time of distribution. The protection does not extinguish a creditor's right to follow the assets into the hands of the persons who received them. It also does not depend on the estate being insolvent.
cluster_text: Doreen died in February. Her will named her daughter Maya as estate trustee and divided the residue equally between Maya and her brother Peter. At the date of death Doreen owned a house worth $620,000 that was subject to a mortgage of $180,000, and a bank account of $40,000 in her own name. She also held shares worth $90,000 in joint tenancy with her son Paul, who survived her. Doreen's funeral bill of $12,000 was unpaid at the date of death, and her final income tax return had not been filed. In May, before paying the funeral bill and before obtaining a clearance certificate, Maya paid the whole residue to herself and Peter. Maya has not yet filed the estate information return and gave no notice to creditors.

question: Maya was appointed estate trustee and the estate certificate was issued to her on 1 June 2026. She has not yet given the Ministry of Finance the prescribed information about the deceased. Within what time must the estate information return be received?

options.A: Within 180 calendar days after the estate certificate is issued.
options.B: Within 30 days after the estate certificate is issued to her.
options.C: Within six months after the last estate asset is distributed.
options.D: Within 90 days after the estate administration tax deposit is paid.

explanation: The correct answer is A (Within 180 calendar days after the estate certificate is issued.): The estate information return must be received by the Ministry of Finance within 180 calendar days after the estate certificate is issued, and it must be filed even if the value of the estate is zero. A return based on an estimated value does not change that deadline, because the estimate is used in the return and an amended return follows once the actual value is known. The other periods named are not the filing deadline for this return.

question: The will appoints Nadia's brother Sam as estate trustee and states that he shall receive $10,000 for his work. The administration takes four years and is unusually demanding. Sam now asks for compensation under the Trustee Act instead. What is the result?

options.A: The tariff of 2.5 per cent applies and replaces the fixed amount.
options.B: The court may award a larger amount if the work turns out to be unusually demanding.
options.C: The fixed amount governs, because the will has already set the compensation.
options.D: Sam may choose whichever of the two amounts is larger for him.

explanation: The correct answer is C (The fixed amount governs, because the will has already set the compensation.): The statutory allowance applies only where the instrument creating the trust does not fix the compensation. Because the will sets a sum for the trustee's work, the court has no power under that provision to increase it. The case law percentages are a guideline for estates where the instrument is silent, and they do not override an amount fixed in the will.

question: A client asks whether one personal surety is enough on a bond for an estate he is administering. The value of the assets of the estate is $85,000 and no insurer is guaranteeing the bond. What should the lawyer advise?

options.A: One personal surety is sufficient where the assets do not exceed $100,000.
options.B: One personal surety is sufficient where the assets do not exceed $50,000.
options.C: Two personal sureties are required whenever the estate exceeds $50,000.
options.D: A trust company must be the surety for every estate of this size.

explanation: The correct answer is A (One personal surety is sufficient where the assets do not exceed $100,000.): Unless the court orders otherwise, one personal surety is sufficient where the value of the assets of the estate does not exceed $100,000. A personal surety must be a resident of Ontario who is not a minor, and neither a registrar of the court nor a lawyer may act as a personal surety. The $50,000 figure belongs to the estate administration tax exemption rather than to the bond rule.

question: The person first entitled to a grant of administration has a large judgment against him and the estate is insolvent. A creditor asks the court to appoint someone else as administrator. Which power does the Estates Act give the court?

options.A: The court may appoint the person it thinks fit where special circumstances make that necessary.
options.B: The court may appoint a trust corporation, but not an individual creditor.
options.C: The court must grant administration to the person first entitled in every case.
options.D: The court may pass over the person entitled only with that person's consent.

explanation: The correct answer is A (The court may appoint the person it thinks fit where special circumstances make that necessary.): Where it appears necessary or convenient because of the insolvency of the estate or other special circumstances, the court is not obliged to grant administration to the person who would otherwise be entitled, and may appoint such person as it thinks fit. A trust corporation may also be appointed, either alone or jointly with another person. The consent of the person passed over is not required, and the court is not bound to follow the order of entitlement.

question: A solicitor is preparing an application for a certificate of appointment of estate trustee with a will. The estate has six residuary beneficiaries and a charity holds a contingent interest. Who must be served with the application and its attachments?

options.A: Any beneficiary who asks the estate trustee for a copy of the will.
options.B: The estate trustee's lawyer, and no beneficiary until the certificate issues.
options.C: Only the residuary beneficiaries, since the charity's interest is contingent.
options.D: Every person entitled to share in the distribution, including the charities.

explanation: The correct answer is D (Every person entitled to share in the distribution, including the charities.): The applicant must serve the application for a certificate of appointment of estate trustee, with its attachments, on every person entitled to share in the distribution of the estate, including charities and contingent beneficiaries. Serving only the residuary beneficiaries would omit the charity and the contingent beneficiaries. The obligation does not depend on a beneficiary asking for the will.

question: Four years and three months have passed since the estate certificate was issued. The estate trustee did not file the estate information return at all. The Minister now proposes to assess tax on a large asset that was omitted from the sworn value. Is that assessment out of time?

options.A: Yes, because the estate has no duty to report assets it did not know about.
options.B: No, the Minister may reassess at any time where the information duty was not met.
options.C: Yes, because four years have passed since the certificate was issued.
options.D: No, the Minister may reassess within six years of the death of the deceased.

explanation: The correct answer is B (No, the Minister may reassess at any time where the information duty was not met.): The Minister may assess or reassess within four years after the day the tax became payable, and that day is the day the estate certificate is issued. The limit does not apply where the Minister establishes that a person failed to comply with the duty to give information, or that there was a misrepresentation attributable to neglect, carelessness or wilful default, or fraud. The four year period therefore does not protect an estate that did not file the required return.

question: A client asks a solicitor who is liable to pay the estate administration tax and when that tax becomes payable. The application for the estate certificate is made in 2026 and the estate is worth $700,000. Which statement is correct?

options.A: It is payable by the estate when the assets are distributed to the beneficiaries.
options.B: It is payable by the estate representative in a representative capacity only.
options.C: It is payable personally by the estate trustee when the certificate issues.
options.D: It is payable by the beneficiaries once they receive their shares of the residue.

explanation: The correct answer is B (It is payable by the estate representative in a representative capacity only.): The tax is payable to the Crown in right of Ontario by the estate of the deceased immediately upon the issuance of an estate certificate, and it is payable by the estate representative in a representative capacity only. That means the representative is not personally liable for the tax itself, even though a failure to give the required information can attract a penalty. The tax is not deferred until the assets are distributed.

question: An applicant can only estimate the value of the estate, so the deposit is based on that estimate. The court accepts a signed undertaking from the applicant. What does the undertaking require the applicant to do at a later date?

options.A: Provide a bond equal to the estimated value of the estate to the court.
options.B: Obtain the Minister's clearance certificate within six months of the death.
options.C: File the estate information return within 30 days of the certificate issuing.
options.D: File a sworn statement of the actual value and pay any extra tax within six months.

explanation: The correct answer is D (File a sworn statement of the actual value and pay any extra tax within six months.): Where the deposit is based on an estimate, the applicant must give the court a signed undertaking to file a sworn statement of the actual total value and to pay any additional tax within six months after giving the undertaking. The undertaking is separate from the estate information return, which is filed within 180 calendar days after the certificate is issued. A clearance certificate relates to income tax and is not what the undertaking promises.

question: A deceased left two wills. The court issues a certificate of appointment of estate trustee with a will limited to the assets referred to in the secondary will. How is the value of the estate determined for estate administration tax?

options.A: The value of all the property that belonged to the deceased at death.
options.B: Only the assets included in the specific will covered by the certificate.
options.C: The combined value of the assets in both wills and the intestate property.
options.D: The value of the assets in the primary will, plus any real property.

explanation: The correct answer is B (Only the assets included in the specific will covered by the certificate.): Where the court issues a certificate of appointment of estate trustee with a will limited to the assets referred to in a will, only the assets included in that specific will are used to calculate the tax. That is what makes the multiple wills strategy effective, because the tax is based on the assets covered by the certificate that is applied for. The tax is not calculated on the combined value of every asset the deceased owned.

question: Ali asks whether the capital gain on the cottage is taxed when he later sells it or at an earlier time. Which statement describes the income tax result of Nadia's death for the cottage that she owned on the date of death?

options.A: The estate reports a capital gain equal to the full fair market value of the cottage.
options.B: She is deemed to have disposed of it at fair market value immediately before death.
options.C: The gain is taxed only when Ali sells the cottage after the death.
options.D: The cottage passes to Ali with no income tax consequence at the death.

explanation: The correct answer is B (She is deemed to have disposed of it at fair market value immediately before death.): Where a taxpayer dies, the taxpayer is deemed to have disposed immediately before death of each capital property for proceeds equal to its fair market value immediately before death. The gain is therefore measured at the death rather than when Ali later sells the cottage, and only the gain, not the whole value, is brought into income. Ali takes the cottage at a cost equal to that fair market value.
cluster_text: Nadia died in January. Her will gave her cottage on Lake Simcoe to her son Ali and the residue of her estate to her daughter Fatima. Nadia owned the cottage alone, and she had rented it out for the last six years. The adjusted cost base of the cottage was $120,000 and its fair market value on the date of death was $410,000. Nadia had not designated the cottage as her principal residence for any year. She also held a registered retirement income fund worth $150,000 with Fatima named as the beneficiary, and a bank account of $60,000 in her own name. Nadia's adult grandson Ben lived with her for the two years before her death and she supported him during that time. Her will left Ben nothing.

question: Nadia's registered retirement income fund was worth $150,000 at the date of her death, and her daughter Fatima was named as the beneficiary before the death. How is the fund treated in the value of the estate for estate administration tax?

options.A: It is included at half its value, because the beneficiary pays the tax.
options.B: It is included only if the estate trustee collects the fund and pays it out.
options.C: It is not included, because it passes to the named beneficiary.
options.D: It is included at its fair market value at the date of death.

explanation: The correct answer is C (It is not included, because it passes to the named beneficiary.): A registered retirement income fund with a valid beneficiary designation passes outside the estate, and the value is not included in the value of the estate for this tax. The same treatment applies to a registered retirement savings plan or a tax free savings account with a beneficiary designation, and to insurance proceeds payable to a named beneficiary. The fund is not included merely because the estate trustee assists with the paperwork.

question: The deemed disposition of the cottage produces a large income tax bill for the estate. The estate trustee would like to spread the payment of that tax over several years rather than pay it at once. Which election is available?

options.A: An election to pay in up to ten equal consecutive annual instalments.
options.B: An election to transfer the tax liability to the beneficiary who receives the cottage.
options.C: An election to defer the tax until the cottage is sold by the beneficiary.
options.D: An election to pay the tax in five equal instalments over five years.

explanation: The correct answer is A (An election to pay in up to ten equal consecutive annual instalments.): The legal representative may elect to pay the tax caused by the death deemed disposition rules in up to 10 equal consecutive annual instalments, with security and interest. The election spreads payment of the tax rather than deferring it until a later sale, and it is not limited to five instalments. The liability remains with the estate and is not transferred to the beneficiary who receives the property.

question: Ben lived with Nadia for two years before her death and she supported him, but the will leaves him nothing. He wants to know whether he has any claim. What is his position under the Succession Law Reform Act in Ontario?

options.A: He may apply for support only if the will names him as a beneficiary.
options.B: He may claim the money she spent on his support as a debt of the estate.
options.C: He may apply for dependant support if he qualifies as a dependant.
options.D: He may claim an intestate share, because he lived in the house with her.

explanation: The correct answer is C (He may apply for dependant support if he qualifies as a dependant.): A grandchild can be a dependant where the deceased demonstrated a settled intention to treat the grandchild as a child of the family and was providing support, or was under a legal obligation to provide support, immediately before the death. The application is made under Part V of the Succession Law Reform Act and does not depend on being named in the will. A person who is not an heir and was not a dependant has no intestate share on these facts.
